references.text: The spies were sent precisely to catch him in his words (ἐπιλαβέσθαι αὐτοῦ λόγου), but here in verse 26 they failed to trap him with any word (οὐκ ἴσχυσαν ἐπιλαβέσθαι τοῦ ῥήματος). Their plan failed. See [ref:Luk 20:20|Luke 20:20].

Matthew's parallel account tells that they were amazed (ἐθαύμασαν) at Jesus' answer and went away. The same reaction of wonder and silence as in Luke's presentation. See [ref:Matt 22:22|Matthew 22:22].
Mark's parallel account uses the expression ἐξεθαύμαζον – they were greatly amazed by him. Jesus' wisdom left his opponents speechless. See [ref:Mark 12:17|Mark 12:17].

On another occasion as well, Jesus' answer brought his opponents to silence: "They could not answer him on this" (οὐκ ἴσχυσαν ἀνταποκριθῆναι). The same pattern of their lacking the strength to refute him. See [ref:Luk 14:6|Luke 14:6].

When Jesus answered his opponents, they were put to shame, while the crowd rejoiced. Here too there is a contrast between the people's reaction and the opponents' silence. See [ref:Luk 13:17|Luke 13:17].

Jesus promises the disciples that he will give them mouth and wisdom which no opponent shall be able to withstand (ἀντιστῆναι) or contradict. Jesus' own answer in 20:25 is an example of just such irresistible wisdom. See [ref:Luk 21:15|Luke 21:15].

After several confrontations with Jesus, no one dared to ask him questions anymore. The opponents' silence (ἐσίγησαν) in Luke 20:26 points forward to this final silence. See [ref:Matt 22:46|Matthew 22:46].

Stephen's opponents "were not able to withstand the wisdom and the Spirit with which he spoke" (οὐκ ἴσχυον ἀντιστῆναι). The same verb (ἰσχύω) and the same pattern: God's wisdom brings opponents to silence. See [ref:Apg 6:10|Acts 6:10].

Isaiah speaks prophetically about those who set traps for the one who pleads a just cause, and with empty pretexts seek to bring down the righteous. The spies' attempt to catch Jesus in his words reflects this pattern. See [ref:Jes 29:21|Isaiah 29:21].
